Blackstone, 3 Commen- taries *123. Cf. Sedgwick, supra, at 53; Suth- erland, supra, at 9 (“If there is no inquiry as to actual damages, or none appear on such inquiry, the legal implication of damage re- mains.”). The common law’s answer in those circumstances was nominal damages: a token amount of money that would vindicate the plaintiff’s rights without violating the rule that any amount of 12 substantial damages had to be proven. See Uzuegbunam v. Prec- zewski, 592 U.S. 279, 286 (II) (A) (141 SCt 792, 209 LE2d 94) (2021). This understanding of nominal damages and their role was well-settled by the time the English common law became a part of Georgia law in the late 1700s. research_issues.question: What limitation period applies under Georgia law to claims for damage to real or personal property, and what exceptions or accrual rules may apply?

propositions.claim: Georgia generally allows four years after the right of action accrues to bring an action for trespass upon or damage to real property, and four years after accrual for injuries to personal property. The cited personal-property code page is the 2024 edition; the real-property provision is shown in the 2025 edition.

For real-property damage, Georgia generally does not delay accrual merely until the owner discovers the damage. A statutory exception applies to specified claims involving damage to a dwelling from synthetic exterior siding: those claims accrue when the damage is discovered or reasonably should have been discovered, subject to the applicable time limits and the statute’s nonrevival provision.

A continuing trespass may support recovery for damages accruing within the four years before suit even if the original entry was earlier; that does not generally revive recovery for older, completed property damage. Whether a nuisance or other repeated harm qualifies as continuing depends on its circumstances.

propositions.claim: Recreational marijuana is not generally legal in Georgia: the Georgia Department of Public Health says marijuana is not legal statewide and that possession by an unauthorized person violates state law. Atlanta’s October 11, 2017 announcement described a city ordinance eliminating jail and capping the local penalty at $75 for possession of one ounce or less; that was a local penalty reduction, not legalization under state law. The announcement is historical, so it does not independently establish whether Atlanta has since changed that ordinance.

Georgia’s medical-cannabis program is limited to eligible patients and caregivers certified through the state registry; Georgia DPH says a physician fully licensed in Georgia, with a principal place of practice in the state, must certify the patient, and a registry card is proof of authorization. The state describes access as requiring annual physician certification.

As of July 1, 2026, Georgia expanded the products available through licensed medical-cannabis dispensaries and independent pharmacies to include oils, tinctures, patches, lotions, capsules, ingestibles, and vaporizer products, including flower for vaporization. Smoking or combustion remains prohibited; the Commission states a limit of 1,200 mg THC per package and a maximum of 12,000 mg THC in a patient’s or caregiver’s possession.

For lawful possession under Georgia’s medical-cannabis law, the Commission identifies three requirements: no more than 12,000 mg total THC, a valid physical or electronic Georgia registry card, and a manufacturer-labeled pharmaceutical container stating the THC amount. Eligibility is limited to the medical conditions and other categories specified by Georgia law.

Federal law separately prohibits knowingly or intentionally manufacturing, distributing, or dispensing a federally controlled substance—or possessing it with intent to do so—unless authorized under federal law. Georgia’s state medical-cannabis authorization is a state-law authorization; the cited federal statute does not itself create an exception for a Georgia registry card.

propositions.claim: A California residential landlord generally must, within 21 calendar days after the tenant vacates, either return the full security deposit or provide an itemized statement of the deductions and refund the remaining balance.

The itemization must state what was deducted and why. For deductions over $125, the landlord generally must provide invoices or receipts; if repair or cleaning work cannot reasonably be completed within 21 days, the landlord may provide a good-faith estimate and must send the receipts within 14 days after the work is completed. California’s Department of Real Estate also describes requirements to provide photographs when deductions are made.

research_issues.question: What is the general statute of limitations for a breach-of-written-contract claim under New York law, and what general accrual rule and exceptions apply?

propositions.claim: New York generally requires an action on a contractual obligation or liability to be commenced within six years. CPLR 213(2) states exceptions, including certain actions governed by other specified statutes or codes; the six-year period is therefore the general rule, not an exception-free rule for every contract claim.

Ordinarily, a breach-of-contract claim accrues when the breach occurs; the period is not postponed merely because the resulting damage happens later or the injured party does not yet know of the breach or injury.

For a contract involving continuing performance, separate breaches may accrue separately, allowing claims for breaches within the six years before filing. The continuing-wrong doctrine is limited to a series of independent, distinct wrongs; continuing effects of one breach do not, by themselves, restart or extend the period for that breach.

research_issues.question: What is the general limitations period under Florida law for filing a negligence personal-injury lawsuit arising from an accident in 2025, and what exceptions or transition rules may affect it?

propositions.claim: For an ordinary negligence personal-injury claim arising from a 2025 accident, Florida Statutes § 95.11(5)(a) sets a two-year limitations period. The period generally runs from accrual; § 95.031(1) says a cause of action accrues when its last element occurs. For an accident injury, that is ordinarily the date of injury, subject to any applicable statutory exception or tolling.

The 2023 change from four years to two years for negligence claims applies to causes of action accruing after March 24, 2023. A claim arising from a 2025 accident falls after that transition date and is therefore subject to the two-year period, rather than the former four-year period.

Potential tolling is governed by Florida Statutes § 95.051, which lists specific grounds, including certain defendant absences or concealment that prevent service, qualifying adjudicated incapacity or minority circumstances, and a pending arbitration concerning the dispute. The statute also provides that a disability or other reason does not toll limitations unless specified by statute. Specialized claims, including medical-malpractice claims, have separate statutory timing provisions and should not automatically be treated as ordinary negligence claims.

propositions.claim: California Penal Code § 632 generally requires the consent of all parties to record a confidential phone call. A communication is confidential when a party has an objectively reasonable expectation that it will not be overheard or recorded. Consent may be implied; § 632 does not require express consent in every case.

propositions.claim: The all-party rule is not limited to confidential calls when a cellular or cordless phone is involved: the California Supreme Court has described § 632.7 as covering intentional, nonconsensual recording of those communications regardless of their content or type. That is a separate statutory protection from § 632’s confidentiality requirement.

New York generally permits recording when at least one party to the conversation consents. Its statutory definitions distinguish wiretapping by a person other than a sender or receiver, which requires lack of consent from either sender or receiver, from mechanical overhearing by a person not present, which requires lack of consent from at least one party. The cited code text is the 2025 edition.

The general rules differ materially: California requires all-party consent for a confidential call, while New York’s statutory framework generally makes one party’s consent sufficient. As a practical precaution for an interstate call involving California and New York, obtaining everyone’s consent avoids relying on New York’s less demanding rule where California law may apply; the governing law for a particular interstate call requires separate analysis.

research_issues.question: Under current U.S. federal law, is Chevron deference still binding when courts interpret statutes administered by federal agencies, and what framework applies instead?
What exceptions or related forms of deference, including agency interpretations of their own regulations, remain relevant under current federal law?

propositions.claim: In Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo (June 28, 2024), the Supreme Court overruled Chevron deference: courts must exercise independent judgment on whether an agency acted within its statutory authority and may not defer merely because the statute is ambiguous. This accords with APA § 706, which directs reviewing courts to decide relevant questions of law and interpret statutory provisions.

An agency’s statutory interpretation may still inform a court’s independent judgment and receive respect to the extent it is persuasive, including where the agency brings relevant experience or expertise. Courts must also respect a statutory delegation of discretionary authority to an agency; that is distinct from binding Chevron deference based on ambiguity alone.

Loper Bright stated that its overruling of Chevron does not itself call into question prior cases’ holdings that specific agency actions are lawful; those holdings remain subject to statutory stare decisis.

For an agency’s interpretation of its own regulation—a different issue from interpreting a statute—Kisor v. Wilkie retained narrowly limited Auer deference. A court may consider deference only after exhausting traditional interpretive tools and finding genuine regulatory ambiguity; the agency’s reading must be reasonable, authoritative, within the agency’s substantive expertise, and reflect fair and considered judgment rather than a convenient litigation position or an unfair surprise.
